question: Team ES2013 weighed several energy sources for their remote. Which options were discussed, which one did they settle on in their third meeting, and was it still the choice in the final costing?
gold: Batteries (including the idea of a rechargeable internal battery), solar power and kinetic energy were discussed. In meeting c the consensus was kinetic energy, if at all possible, and in meeting d the final costing still used a single kinetic energy source.
answer: Team ES2013 discussed standard AA batteries (including a rechargeable internal battery with a docking station), a wind-up mechanism, kinetic energy and solar power; solar was dropped because it needs energy storage (too heavy and costly) and doesn't work in the dark. In the third meeting, led by Speaker A (Project Manager), they reached a consensus to use kinetic energy if at all possible, and kinetic was still the choice in the fourth meeting's recap and final costing, though Speaker C (User Interface Designer) noted the energy side was not fully developed.

judge_note: Nothing material. The candidate covers batteries (including the rechargeable internal battery), solar and kinetic energy, and says kinetic was the consensus in meeting 3 and still the choice in the final costing. The extra details (wind-up mechanism, speaker roles, reasons solar was dropped) don't contradict the reference.

question: In Team IS1006, who first proposed making the remote out of titanium and why, what was said about rubber as an alternative, and which material did the final design keep?
gold: Speaker B proposed titanium in meeting b, for a baby-proof, unbreakable remote with a good style. In meeting c rubber was weighed (Speaker D liked its spongy feel; Speaker C said rubber is expensive and hard to shape), but in meeting d they stuck with titanium.
answer: Speaker B (User Interface Designer) first proposed titanium in the second meeting (IS1006b), arguing it would make the remote baby-proof, with a really good style, unbreakable and very universal. In the conceptual meeting (IS1006c), Speaker C (Industrial Designer) said the team would mainly use titanium because rubber is expensive and makes the shapes difficult, while Speaker B suggested a compromise of a titanium body with some rubber parts to feel better. The final design (IS1006d) kept titanium, with Speaker C saying 'we want to stick to titanium'.

citations.quote: to make a baby-proof remote control it got to be a titanium. It's a really good style, it going to be look like like this. It is unbreakable and it is very universal.
We'll use mainly for titanium rubber is expensive and also it's bit difficult to do all the shapes uh.
Material, we want to stick to titanium.

judge_note: Titanium proposer (Speaker B, meeting b, with baby-proof/unbreakable/style reasons) and the final titanium choice are correct. On rubber, the candidate gives Speaker C's point (expensive, hard to shape) but omits Speaker D, who liked rubber's spongy feel. It attributes a rubber-parts compromise to Speaker B instead, which is not in the reference.

question: What energy source did Team ES2015 choose, what happened to the idea of a solar backup, and what did the energy source cost in their final costing?
gold: They chose kinetic energy (Speaker B, the Industrial Designer, favoured it in meeting c). A solar backup was suggested in meeting c but dropped in favour of going fully kinetic. In meeting d the kinetic source was costed at three Euros, described as quite a large expense.
answer: Team ES2015 chose kinetic (shake-powered) energy, confirmed by Speaker A (Project Manager) in the third meeting as fully kinetic with no battery backup. Speaker B (Industrial Designer) had floated a solar backup instead of a battery, but it was dropped and in the final meeting was said to be unaffordable. In the final costing, the kinetic source was counted at three Euros, which Speaker A (Project Manager) called quite a large expense.

question: Team IS1004 considered both an LCD screen and speech recognition. Which was ruled out first, in which meeting was the other ruled out, and what arguments were made against the LCD?
gold: Speech recognition was ruled out first, in meeting b, while the LCD was left open. The LCD was dropped in meeting c, because of cost against the 25 Euro price target and because Speaker D (Marketing Expert) argued it needed an internet connection and more requirements.
answer: Speech recognition was ruled out first, in IS1004b, while the LCD was left open. The LCD was ruled out second, in the third meeting (IS1004c), where Speaker A (Project Manager) said the team was forgetting about it. The arguments against the LCD were that the 25 Euro target price could not cover both an LCD and speech recognition, so the TV screen was proposed for feedback instead; Speaker D (Marketing Expert) said an LCD needs an internet connection and extra components; and Speaker A noted a banana-shaped remote leaves little room for one. IS1004d confirms the final design had no LCD.

question: What power source did Team IS1004's industrial designer propose, and what happened to the solar cells in the final meeting and why?
gold: Speaker C (Industrial Designer) proposed rechargeable batteries with a base (docking) station plus solar cells. In meeting d Speaker B (User Interface Designer) argued solar cells were no longer necessary with a recharging base station, and the team decided against them.
answer: Speaker C (Industrial Designer) proposed usual batteries that could be rechargeable via a base station, plus solar cells for use when lighting conditions are good (meeting IS1004c). question: Did Team ES2005 keep speech recognition in their final design, and what happened to the screen idea and why?
gold: Yes: speech recognition was voted in during meeting b and the final design in meeting d is mainly speech-operated, with buttons on the flip side. The LCD screen was dropped: in meeting c Speaker D argued it was too expensive for the 12.50 Euro budget and not right for an easy-to-use product, so the final design has no screen.
answer: Yes, Team ES2005 kept speech recognition: Speaker C (Project Manager) settled on it after the second meeting, and in the final meeting Speaker D (User Interface Designer) presented a prototype that works mainly by speech recognition, with buttons on the back. The screen idea was dropped: the TFT screen was rejected in the second meeting because, as Speaker A (Industrial Designer) warned, remotes get thrown around and a screen would likely break, and the LCD was rejected in the third meeting as too expensive for the budget and at odds with an easy-to-use remote, so the final design was noted as missing the screen.

judge_note: Nothing key is missing or wrong. Speech recognition was kept (decided in meeting b, with a mainly speech-operated final design and buttons on the back). The LCD was dropped in meeting c as too expensive and not easy to use. The candidate does not name Speaker D as the one who argued against the LCD or give the 12.50 Euro figure, and its extra detail about the TFT screen in meeting b is unverified, but neither affects the key facts.

question: What production cost limit was Team IS1000 working to, what did their more advanced design with speech recognition cost in the final meeting, and how much of that was the speech recognition?
gold: The limit was 12.50 Euros per unit (stated in meeting a and repeated in meeting d as non-negotiable). The advanced design came to 16 Euros, out of budget, of which the speech recognition system was about 3 Euros (about 13 without it); the basic version was about 8 Euros.
answer: Team IS1000 worked to a maximum production cost of twelve euros fifty cents per unit, set by Speaker B (Project Manager) in the first meeting. In the final meeting their more advanced design with speech recognition was costed at about sixteen euros, of which speech recognition was about three euros (roughly a fifth), so without it the design came to thirteen euros; they ultimately dropped it and the LCD and went with the basic design at about twelve euros.

It also attributes the limit to meeting a only and omits that it was repeated in meeting d as non-negotiable, which is minor. The basic-design cost is a wrong claim about a key fact.

question: Team TS3012 had agreed to put both an LCD screen and speech recognition in their remote. What happened to these in their final meeting, and what reason was given?
gold: Changed finances forced a cut in meeting d: Speaker A (Project Manager) proposed taking out speech recognition and keeping the LCD, because about ninety percent of users favoured an LCD display but only sixty percent favoured speech recognition.
answer: In the final meeting (TS3012d), Speaker A (Project Manager) said the design came to seventeen Euros in production cost, above the permitted twelve and a half, so speech recognition was dropped from the base product while the LCD screen was kept because it has more customer support. Speaker C (Industrial Designer) added that speech recognition cannot be done at this price, so customers who want it must pay more.

citations.quote: You have the total of seventeen Euros in production cost, which is higher than the twelve and a half that we are permitted to use.

then they must be prepared to pu to pay more, because it's cannot be done for this.

judge_note: The outcome is right: speech recognition was dropped and the LCD kept. The reason differs from the reference. The reference says finances changed and the choice rested on user preference, with about 90% favouring an LCD and only 60% favouring speech recognition. The candidate instead gives a production cost of 17 Euros against a 12.5 limit and says only that the LCD has 'more customer support'. It leaves out the 90% vs 60% figures. The cost and budget numbers are not in the reference, so they are unsupported.
